findings.title: Survivor tracker drops descendants spawned after the first read, so the mid-run hold releases early
findings.scenario: A workstation-approved session's root exits. Read 1 finds child C (pid 200, ppid 100) alive, so lingering = [C]. C then starts grandchild G (pid 300, ppid 200) that outlives C. result.reasoning:
Not refuted. The defect is real and reproduces. Probe (throwaway, deleted; no repo test run, so no test-results change): TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors.call on a fake with scripted reads [pid 200 ppid 100 alive], [pid 300 ppid 200 alive], [] gives read1 lingering=[200] and read2 lingering entry ABSENT, with reads stopping at 2 (no further re-check scheduled). Code: manager.server.ts:1717 uses survivors(known, rows) when known is set, so only the set from read 1 is ever re-checked. Line 1709 orphan logic only follows children of rootPid, and descendants(rows, rootPid) returns [] once the root row is gone. So a grandchild (ppid = a tracked process that exited) is never re-derived. Its own code comment at manager.server.ts:1642 and the test name F01-R36 both promise that descendants keep the session live until none survives; that is violated here.
Realistic trigger: the tracked child must spawn a long-lived grandchild after read 1 (reads are 10 s apart) and then exit before the next read. Windows ppid remains stale, so the grandchild is still identifiable but untracked. Once lingering is cleared, liveCodeExecutions (manager.server.ts:2311) no longer counts the session and bus.server.ts:165 remoteMutationHeld returns null. A paired-device one-time filesystem.write then proceeds while workstation-approved code is still running.
Mitigating factors that keep this at MEDIUM and not higher: the write must still be an exact planned in-envelope step; no device code execution path is opened (the review gate and desktop grants are unaffected); and the timing window is narrow. It is still a reproducible break of the documented mid-run hold invariant, so it is not an owner-policy disposition or accepted limitation.
Suggested fix, matching the finding: on each read, keep still-alive members of the set, then add descendants (born-after check) of each still-alive tracked process and orphans of the root, and keep the entry while the set is non-empty. Add a test where the survivor is a grandchild spawned after read 1 whose intermediate parent exits.

The core defect is real and reproduces. Probe (throwaway folder under the OS temp dir, now deleted; no repo files written, no test run) drove TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors with a fake receiver and scripted process tables. Read 1 returned [pid 200, ppid 100] and the entry became [200]. Read 2 returned [pid 300, ppid 200] (grandchild alive, intermediate gone) and the entry was CLEARED. Mechanism: src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1717 computes survivors(known, rows), which only re-checks the set from read 1, so the grandchild is never added. Once the intermediate exits, the grandchild cannot be re-derived from ppid: on Windows ppid is not reparented, and orphans() at 1706-1711 only follows the root pid chain and ppid==rootPid children. So the proposed fix ("add descendants of each still-alive tracked process") would not catch this exact scenario, because the tracked intermediate is dead by read 2. A correct fix would accumulate the tracked pid set across reads and admit rows whose ppid is an already-tracked pid (including dead ones) and whose createdAt is not earlier than that parent's.

Why I rate it LOW rather than the claimed MEDIUM: (1) the window is narrow. The grandchild must be spawned after read 1 by an intermediate that exits before read 2, about 10 s apart. Anything alive at read 1 is caught, and any process in the periodic tree snapshot is caught. (2) Impact is limited to the mid-run hold in bus.server.ts:165 and manager.server.ts remoteMutationHeld (2322). The device write it releases is still an exact planned, in-envelope, device-approved step, so it does not give a device code execution or action outside the envelope, which is the owner-policy test. It does break the hold's stated invariant (a device change should not land under live workstation-approved code), and that is why this is not refuted outright. The probe confirms the premise; the severity is overstated.

findings.title: Mid-run hold and review gate miss workstation-approved provider sessions whose descendants outlive the tracked tree
findings.scenario: A workstation-approved shell-capable provider session (Claude write or Codex) starts a detached background process. Its launcher child exits, and the server it started survives. watchSurvivors re-checks only the previous alive set (survivors(known, rows)), never re-expanding it to new descendants, so the survivor is dropped from lingering and liveCodeExecutions() no longer reports live code. A paired device (for example via an in-envelope planned filesystem.write in a device-approved Mission, which needs no ask) then writes a project file the surviving process loads. remoteMutationHeld() sees no live code and lets the write land. The review gate (pendingRemoteChanges) only blocks new bus runs and launches, so the already-running process executes device-authored content with no workstation decision. Probed with the real TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors (fake process tables): (1) launcher 4343 (ppid root 4242) alive, then exits leaving server 4444 (ppid 4343) alive -> lingering entry REMOVED, server untracked. (2) Grandchild born after the last 15 s tree sample whose parent is already dead -> NOT TRACKED. Controls: a child of the root still alive -> tracked; a grandchild present in the last sample -> tracked. So coverage holds only while the intermediate parent is alive at the first post-exit read and the descendant predates the last sample.
findings.evidence: Probe run in a mkdtemp folder under %TEMP% (deleted afterwards): 'A daemon after last sample, intermediate dead: -> NOT TRACKED'; 'B intermediate still alive (control): -> tracked: 4343,4444'; 'C daemon in last sample: -> tracked: 4444'; re-check probe: 'reads: 2 | lingering after launcher exits: REMOVED (server 4444 still alive, not tracked)'. Code: manager.server.ts:1706-1710 (orphans only follows ppid==root), :1715-1718 (re-check uses survivors(known, rows) and deletes on empty), :2311-2319 (liveCodeExecutions reads lingering only), bus.server.ts:603-604 (remoteMutationHeld hold depends on liveCodeExecutions). Snapshot cadence watchTree is 2 s initial then 15 s (manager.server.ts ~1663-1700). terminal.exec runs use the owned job-object path (process.server.ts:65, owned-process-group.server.ts) and were not analysed natively, so they are not claimed here.
findings.recommendation: Re-expand the tracked set on every check: union survivors(known) with orphans(rows) and with every descendant of any alive tracked process (descendants by pid+birth time), and keep lingering non-empty until a read finds no process that descends from the root or from any tracked survivor. Consider sampling the process table at the exit of each shell-capable session and at a shorter interval while it runs. Add a regression test for launcher-exits-leaving-grandchild (and the 'born after last sample' case) to F01-R36.

Confirmed by reading and probing (no repo tests run; probe folder created and removed under the OS temp dir):
- authorization.server.ts:162 isTrustedLocalActor is exactly "workstation". authorityFor (163-165) returns kind "remote" for any other actor. isRemoteEnvelope (170-175) is true for grantedBy "test".

Why the severity is LOW, not MEDIUM:
- Remote is the fail-closed direction. Nothing that was trusted before becomes untrusted in production, and no device gains authority. Device actors are "device:<id>" and production actors are "workstation" or device, so no production path passes "test".
- The effect is that the affected test fixtures (agent-recovery.test.ts, agent-runtime.test.ts, and similar) stall at desktop-required asks. The Codex read fixtures in agent-recovery (about lines 222 and 263) are the likely failures. That is a test-hygiene and correctness problem for the suite, not a device-authority or code-execution hole.
- The pass or fail of those tests is unverified, as the finding says. The fix is to change the fixture actors to "workstation" where a trusted local caller is intended, then run the suites.

The behaviour change is real and confirmed by code. authorization.server.ts:162 makes only actor === "workstation" trusted-local, and :163-164 gives every other grantor a remote envelope with codeExecution "desktop_only". isRemoteEnvelope (:170-175) agrees. Agent envelopes take grantedBy from the start actor: agent-runtime.server.ts:152-168 calls missions.approve(..., actor), and manager.server.ts:800 calls envelopeFrom(..., by). So agents.start(id, "test") creates a remote envelope.

The breakage is concrete for agent-recovery.test.ts A15 (lines 300-345). The restart walk at manager.server.ts:4145-4146 revokes every live remote envelope and puts the mission in waiting_for_user (about :4256). The test then calls env.missions.retry(missionId, "test") at :339. retry() at manager.server.ts:3864-3880 throws "The mission authorization expired or was revoked; replan to approve it again." when the envelope is revoked. So A15 should fail at :339, one line before the finding's :343 respond, and the finding's line reference is slightly off. This is an inference from code paths, since I did not run the suite.

Production is not affected. Every production approval path passes "workstation" or a "device:<id>" actor. project-service.server.ts:101 uses "workstation". The trigger path creates drafts only and calls no approve. http.server.ts passes the device or workstation principal. So the effect is limited to test suites that use "test" as an actor. The change is fail-closed, not a security weakening. The MEDIUM rating overstates it, and LOW fits a test-suite regression with no security or production impact. findings.title: Surviving-process tracking drops descendants spawned after the first check, lifting the device mid-run hold
findings.scenario: A workstation-approved provider session ends while a launcher child is still alive (orphan of the exited root). The first check (orphans) records the launcher. The launcher then starts a long-lived server (e.g. a dev server that hot-reloads src files) that is NOT in the last 15 s process-tree snapshot, and the launcher exits. Every later check runs survivors(known, rows) only (line 1717), never re-scanning descendants of live survivors or orphans of the root. Once the launcher is gone, survivors() is empty, line 1718 deletes the lingering entry, and MissionManager.liveCodeExecutions() (manager.server.ts ~2311) returns []. remoteMutationHeld() (~2330) then no longer holds a paired-device Mission mutation, so a device-approved filesystem.write to a project file (non-config path, allowed remotely) lands while the surviving workstation-approved server is running and can load the device-chosen content. Descendant discovery also never reaches processes whose intermediate parent exited before the snapshot (process-tree.server.ts descendants() requires a live chain from the root; orphans() only matches direct children of the root).
findings.evidence: Probe (throwaway folder, real TaskManager/MissionManager, stubbed readProcesses): launcher 200 (ppid = exited root 100) alive at session end; dev-server 501 spawned by 200 at t=2s. At t=12s launcher exited, dev-server alive. After the 10 s recheck: lingering has t-live=false and liveCodeExecutions() = [] while dev-server.exe is still in the process table. Control session (child 310 existed at first check) kept lingering=[early-node.exe(310)] at t=21.5s, so the defect is the re-check logic. Relevant code: manager.server.ts:1699-1721 (watchSurvivors/check), manager.server.ts:2311-2331 (liveCodeExecutions, remoteMutationHeld), process-tree.server.ts:25-36 (descendants).
findings.recommendation: On every re-check, rediscover descendants of each live survivor and the root's orphans (not only survivors of the previous set), and keep the entry until the whole tree is gone. Consider tracking by job object or process group on Windows so detached children cannot escape. Add a regression test that spawns a late child under a launcher which exits after the session ends and asserts the hold stays until that child exits.

findings.title: One-time allowance executes after the workstation envelope has expired
findings.scenario: decide() returns allow for context.oneTime at line 354, before the envelope expiry check at line 362. The remote-envelope expiry check at line 353 precedes it, but for workstation envelopes an approvedOnce allowance (given by a device or the workstation before expiry) still allows the step after expiresAt. Capability launches have no envelope expiry check (the tick only compares startedAt plus the runtime limit, manager.server.ts ~907-920), so a step that was approved before expiry and is waiting for a concurrency slot, or whose Mission runtime limit outlasts the envelope, runs after the envelope expired. Device answers are refused after expiry (manager.server.ts ~2041), so exposure is the answer-to-launch gap, not a fresh device approval.
findings.evidence: Probe with decide(): workstation envelope with expiresAt in the past plus oneTime:true returns allow ('The user allowed this invocation...'); the same envelope without oneTime returns ask ('The mission authorization expired.'); a device envelope expired with oneTime:true returns ask ('The remote mission authorization expired.'). Relevant lines: authorization.server.ts:353-354 and 362.
findings.recommendation: Move the expiry (and revocation) checks ahead of the oneTime allowance for every envelope, or re-check envelope expiry in the launch path for capability steps before the bus runs them.

findings.title: Browser downloads are recorded as project changes at the Mission folder path
findings.scenario: bus.remoteMutationStarted records a remote change with path = request.cwd when params.path is not a string. browser.download (WRITE, in MUTATIONS) takes url/selector, not path, so the recorded change is the Mission folder rather than the downloaded file. The file actually lands in dataDirectory/artifacts/<mission>/downloads (browser.server.ts:237-252), and remoteChanges() (manager.server.ts ~2285) later reports the literal string 'browser.download' as the path. The Host-wide code gate still blocks code runs while the row exists, so this is misleading review content (the round-6 'wrong name' claim is correct), not a gate bypass.

result.reasoning:
The defect is real and reproduced, but the claimed HIGH severity is not supported: the impact is a bypass of the mid-run hold on device-attributable in-envelope writes, not device-driven code execution.

Code (src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1699-1721): watchSurvivors computes `alive = known ? survivors(known, rows) : orphans(rows)` and then `setTimeout(() => void check(alive))`. Once a set is established, rechecks only test identity of the previously recorded PIDs. They never rediscover children of a live survivor or children of a dead intermediate. The code comment at ~line 1642 says descendants of the ended root "stay live code until none survives", so this contradicts the module's own stated contract.

Probe (throwaway temp dir, real TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors called on a stub `this`, a 5 ms setTimeout override, readProcesses stubbed; temp dir deleted afterwards, no repo files touched, no tests run):
- S1 (late child of live launcher): launcher 200 (ppid 100) present at first check, so lingering=[200]. Dev 501 (ppid 200) appears later. Launcher exits. Lingering becomes absent while 501 is still alive, so liveCodeExecutions() no longer counts it.
- S2 (chain broken before first check): rows=[501 with dead ppid 200], empty snapshot. lingering is absent immediately while 501 is alive.
- S3 (control, child present at first check): lingering=[200,501], then [501] after the launcher exits. This is correct, so the defect is in the recheck logic.

Why MEDIUM and not HIGH: the lifted hold only affects device-attributable MUTATIONS requests (bus.server.ts:165). Those are still bounded to planned, in-envelope, non-sensitive steps, and the device gets no shell or code-execution authority. The execution is performed by a process the workstation already approved. The consequence is that a device-approved in-envelope file write can land under a still-running, workstation-approved hot-reloading server that outlived its session. This is a real gate bypass and a correctness problem, so the finding is not refuted. The existing test F01-R36 covers only a direct detached child and misses both shapes.

The finding holds. Code reading and two probes (real TaskManager.prototype.watchSurvivors called on a stub object with a controlled setTimeout queue and stubbed readProcesses, in a mkdtemp folder that was then deleted; the repo was not edited and no repo tests were run).

Probe 1, late-spawned server: at t=0 the table holds only the launcher 200 (ppid 100, the exited root). At t=2 launcher 200 spawns node 501 (ppid 200), which is absent from the snapshot. At t=10 lingering is [200]. At t=12 the launcher exits and 501 stays alive. At t=20 lingering is [] and 501 is still in the table. The cause is manager.server.ts:1717, where every re-check after the first runs `survivors(known, rows)`, so descendants of live survivors are never rediscovered. Line 1718 then deletes the entry.

Probe 2, grandchild with an exited intermediate: root 100 has exited, its child 200 exits before the first check, and grandchild 777 (ppid 200) stays alive. The result is lingering = [] on the first check, with 777 alive. orphans() (manager.server.ts:1700-1712) only matches direct children of the root and descends only through live parents, and process-tree.server.ts:25-36 descendants() requires a live chain. So even the first check misses this shape.

Consequence: liveCodeExecutions() (manager.server.ts:2311-2320) counts only tasks.sessions and tasks.lingering, and the session is removed from sessions in the finally block (~1640-1644). remoteMutationHeld() (manager.server.ts:2322-2332) therefore returns null, and bus.server.ts:165 stops holding a device-attributable Mission mutation while the workstation-approved server still runs. Directly, bus.liveCode (bus.server.ts:308/349) covers only the terminal.exec adapter's lifetime, so it does not cover this path. This contradicts the round-6 claim (B) that the mid-run hold keeps device mutations asking the workstation.

Caveats that do not refute it: the write itself is a planned in-envelope step, so the device does not pick arbitrary content, and impact requires a still-running server that reloads project files. The 15 s snapshot window is only partially protective, because a server spawned during the last tick interval is missed too. Lingering state is in memory, which is listed as an accepted limitation only for Host restarts, not for this in-session gap. The defect defeats the owner-stated mid-run hold, so HIGH is appropriate. Suggested fix: on every re-check, union orphans(rows) with survivors(known, rows) and rediscover descendants of each live survivor.

The decide()-level claim is real. Probe (temp dir, decide imported by file URL, deleted afterwards): workstation envelope with expiresAt in the past and oneTime=true returns allow ("The user allowed this invocation..."); oneTime=false returns ask ("The mission authorization expired."). Ordering confirmed at authorization.server.ts:353-354 (remote-only expiry check, then oneTime allow) before :362 (workstation expiry check). Remote envelopes are safe because line 353 precedes the one-time allow.

The launch-level scenario as written is largely blocked. manager.server.ts:912-921 (tick) fails the Mission with budget_exceeded when startedAt + min(envelope.budget.maxRuntimeMs, cached maxMissionRuntimeMs) has passed, and it does not admit steps in that case. For a workstation envelope, expiresAt = grantedAt + min(config at grant, budget.maxRuntimeMs) (authorization.server.ts:105). startedAt is set at manager.server.ts:847 during approve() at line 839, a few ms after the grant, so the runtime deadline and the envelope deadline coincide. A slot-waiting approved step therefore cannot launch after expiry under unchanged config. The only post-expiry launch window needs startedAt to lag the grant, or cached maxMissionRuntimeMs to be raised after grant (configure is workstation-only per commands.server.ts REMOTE set, but the owner can do it). Under that owner-driven condition, a device's pre-expiry one-time approval (device answers are refused after expiry at manager.server.ts:2041) could execute after expiry until the new deadline. Agent Missions are covered: envelope.expiresAt is min'd with agentic.expires_at (manager.server.ts:810) and agenticIdentityViolation returns "Agentic delegation expired." (manager.server.ts:2542), which becomes an ask before the oneTime allow (authorization.server.ts:357). A device cannot create a new approval after expiry, and the code-execution gates are unaffected by this. So this is a real expiry-ordering defect with a narrow, owner-dependent launch exposure and no device-initiated code execution. Not a listed disposition. Severity LOW, not refuted. The reviewer's stated scenario (slot-waiting step runs after expiry) is overstated; the fix should move the workstation expiry/revocation check ahead of the oneTime allow, or add an expiry check in the launch path.

Not refuted. The gap is real and reproduces with the actual descendants/survivors helpers, using the same logic as the orphans() closure in src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1706-1713.

Code path: watchSurvivors (manager.server.ts:1699) runs check(null) at session end, which calls orphans(rows). orphans() takes descendants(rows, rootPid), which returns [] once the root is gone (process-tree.server.ts:26-27). It then takes direct children of rootPid, and survivors() of the last processTree snapshot. A grandchild whose intermediate parent has also exited, and which was born after the last snapshot, is in none of these sets.

Probe (temp folder under the OS temp dir, deleted afterwards): root 4242 absent, intermediate 4343 absent, grandchild 4444 (ppid 4343, alive), snapshot = [root, mid]. Result: orphans() = []. With the root alive, the same rows give [4242, 4343, 4444]. With 4444 already in the snapshot, the result is [4444]. This matches the finding's probe p5.

Precondition check: the miss needs the intermediate to exit and the root to exit inside the window between the last 15 s tree snapshot and session end. That is narrow but reachable with a launch-and-exit pattern. The consequence is that lingering is not set, so MissionManager.liveCodeExecutions (bunny-missions/manager.server.ts:2312) omits that session and remoteMutationHeld stops holding device mutations while workstation-approved code still runs. That weakens the mid-run hold, but it does not give a device code execution or an action outside its own envelope, and it is not one of the listed owner-policy dispositions. Hence LOW, not refuted.

Confirmed the decide() ordering: authorization.server.ts:351 (agenticViolation ask), 352-353 (remote-only expiry ask), 354 (oneTime allow), 362 (workstation expiry ask). Probe (temp dir, deleted): workstation envelope expired + oneTime=true -> allow; expired + oneTime=false -> ask "The mission authorization expired."; device envelope expired + oneTime=true -> ask "The remote mission authorization expired." So the mechanism exists for non-agentic workstation envelopes. Agentic missions are covered: agenticCheck -> agenticIdentityViolation checks envelope.expiresAt (manager.server.ts ~2547) and that becomes agenticViolation, which precedes oneTime. Launch path (manager.server.ts ~913-920, runDeterministic) has no expiry check, as claimed.
Exploitability is narrow. A one-time allowance is only created by a respond() on a running, pre-expiry ask (respond itself does not check workstation expiry, and deviceRequestRefusal refuses post-expiry device answers at ~2041). The step then launches in the same schedule() call unless the launch is deferred. Expiry is grantedAt + min(cached maxMissionRuntimeMs at grant, budget), while the tick's runtime limit is startedAt + min(budget, cached now). With default config and start() called in the same approve(), startedAt ~= grantedAt so the runtime limit fires at about the same moment as expiry and the tick fails the mission before a deferred step launches. A gap needs either (a) startedAt later than grantedAt, which a device can produce only via approve(start:false) on a remote envelope (safe, since remote is refused at line 353), or a workstation approve(start:false) followed by a device mission.start, plus (b) concurrency saturation (STEP_LIVE = running/verifying) deferring the approved step past expiry. Owner config raise mid-run would also widen the gap, but mission.configure is workstation-only (REMOTE set in commands.server.ts). The workstation post-expiry allow_once path is the deliberate re-approval flow, so it is not a finding. The device cannot start, extend or choose an action beyond its single pre-expiry answer on an exact planned non-sensitive step, so impact is a time-bound violation of at most the runtime-limit gap. Not refuted; LOW is the appropriate severity. Repo status unchanged (26 entries, matching the start snapshot); no repo tests run.

Not refuted. The mechanism is real and broader than the finding states. src/lib/bunny-host/manager.server.ts:1706-1713 builds orphans(rows) from three sources: descendants(rows, rootPid) (line 1708), direct children of rootPid born after the root (line 1709-1710), and survivors of the last snapshot (line 1711). descendants() in process-tree.server.ts:25-38 only walks from a live root through live parent pids, so a grandchild whose intermediate shell exited is unreachable. The snapshot is also chain-based (manager.server.ts:1658, descendants(rows, pid)), so such a grandchild is never captured by any snapshot taken after the intermediate exited. The missed window is therefore not limited to "born after the last snapshot"; any detached grandchild whose intermediate parent has exited before the session ends is untracked after session end.
